entries.c7f6def9d921e672e12d6e79c5188cb71caab85e: <div eID="gen17624" type="x-p"/> <title type="x-s">Introduction</title> <div sID="gen17625" type="introduction"/> <div sID="gen17626" type="x-p"/> <div eID="gen17626" type="x-p"/> <div eID="gen17625" type="introduction"/> <div sID="gen17627" type="x-p"/> Elihu begins with an exhortation to Job's friends, <reference osisRef="Job.34.1-Job.34.4">Job 34:1-4</reference>; charges Job with accusing God of acting unrighteously, which he shows is impossible, <reference osisRef="Job.34.5-Job.34.12">Job 34:5-12</reference>; points out the power and judgments of the Almighty, vv. 13-30; shows how men should address God, and how irreverently Job has acted, <reference osisRef="Job.34.31-Job.34.37">Job 34:31-37</reference>.
entries.83f71e2bef7ecf6a2cb161d00863840741b65ffe: <hi type="bold">Verse 3</hi> <div eID="gen17627" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen17628" type="x-p"/> The ear trieth words - I do not think, with Calmet, that the inward ear, or judgment, is meant simply. The Asiatics valued themselves on the nice and harmonious collection of words, both in speaking and in writing; and perhaps it will be found here that Elihu labors as much for harmonious versification as for pious and weighty sentiments. To connect sense with sound was an object of general pursuit among the Hebrew, Arabic, and Persian poets; and so fond are the latter of euphony, that they often sacrifice both sense and sentiment to it; and some of the Greek poets are not exempt from this fault.
entries.5cb780270f7c7847c10155d4037a734b53008f02: <hi type="bold">Verse 4</hi> <div eID="gen17628" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen17629" type="x-p"/> Let us choose to us judgment - Let us not seek the applause of men, nor contend for victory. Let our aim be to obtain correct views and notions of all things; and let us labor to find out what is good.
entries.f1d784e1fb23823a0e596b9c9090edbb15fdb646: <hi type="bold">Verse 5</hi> <div eID="gen17629" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen17630" type="x-p"/> Job hath said, I am righteous - Job had certainly said the words attributed to him by Elihu, particularly in <reference osisRef="Job.27.2">Job 27:2</reference>, etc., but it was in vindication of his aspersed character that he had asserted his own righteousness, and in a different sense to that in which Elihu appears to take it up. He asserted that he was righteous quoad the charges his friends had brought against him. And he never intimated that he had at all times a pure heart, and had never transgressed the laws of his Maker. It is true also that he said, God hath taken away my judgment; but he most obviously does not mean to charge God with injustice, but to show that he had dealt with him in a way wholly mysterious, and not according to the ordinary dispensations of his providence; and that he did not interpose in his behalf, while his friends were overwhelming him with obloquy and reproach.
entries.cf238c67379efbac941da338daee69f8d8bcc975: <hi type="bold">Verse 6</hi> <div eID="gen17630" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen17631" type="x-p"/> Should I lie against my right? - Should I acknowledge myself the sinner which they paint me, and thus lie against my right to assert and maintain my innocence? <div eID="gen17631" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen17632" type="x-p"/> My wound is incurable without transgression - If this translation is correct, the meaning of the place is sufficiently evident. In the tribulation which I endure, I am treated as if I were the worst of culprits; and I labor under incurable maladies and privations, though without any cause on my part for such treatment. This was all most perfectly true; it is the testimony which God himself gives of Job, that "he was a perfect and upright man, fearing God and eschewing evil;" and that "Satan had moved the Lord against him, to destroy him, Without a Cause. See <reference osisRef="Job.1.1">Job 1:1</reference>; <reference osisRef="Job.2.3">Job 2:3</reference>. <div eID="gen17632" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen17633" type="x-p"/> The Chaldee translates thus: - "On account of my judgment, I will make the son of man a liar, who sends forth arrows without sin." <div eID="gen17633" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen17634" type="x-p"/> Mr. Good thus: - "Concerning my cause I am slandered; <div eID="gen17634" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen17635" type="x-p"/> He hath reversed my lot without a trespass." <div eID="gen17635" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen17636" type="x-p"/> The latter clause is the most deficient, אנוש חצי בלי פשע; Miss Smith's translation of which is the best I have met with: "A man cut off, without transgression." The word חצי chitstsi, which we translate my wound, signifies more literally, my arrow; and if we take it as a contracted noun, חצי chitstsey for חצים chitstsim, it means calamities. אנוש anush, which we translate incurable, may be the noun enosh, wicked, miserable man; and then the whole may be read thus: "A man of calamities without transgression." I suffer the punishment of an enemy to God, while free from transgression of this kind.
entries.9003795111db5d85c000582b3453fec39c778c45: <hi type="bold">Verse 7</hi> <div eID="gen17636" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen17637" type="x-p"/> Drinketh up scorning like water? - This is a repetition of the charge made against Job by Eliphaz, <reference osisRef="Job.15.16">Job 15:16</reference>. It is a proverbial expression, and seems to be formed, as a metaphor, from a camel drinking, who takes in a large draught of water, even the most turbid, on its setting out on a journey in a caravan, that it may serve it for a long time. Job deals largely in scorning; he fills his heart with it.
entries.9b5a2571c2b8c80d7d882fc6a14d77409286f431: <hi type="bold">Verse 8</hi> <div eID="gen17637" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen17638" type="x-p"/> Which goeth in company with the workers of iniquity - This is an allusion to a caravan: all kinds of persons are found there; but yet a holy and respectable man might be found in that part of the company where profligates assembled. But surely this assertion of Elihu was not strictly true; and the words literally translated, will bear a less evil meaning: "Job makes a track ארח arach, to join fellowship, לחברה lechebrah, with the workers of iniquity;" i.e., Job's present mode of reasoning, when he says, "I am righteous, yet God hath taken away my judgment," is according to the assertion of sinners, who say, "There is no profit in serving God; for, if a man be righteous, he is not benefited by it, for God does not vindicate a just man's cause against his oppressors." By adopting so much of their creed, he intimates that Job is taking the steps that lead to fellowship with them. See <reference osisRef="Job.34.9">Job 34:9</reference>.
entries.9fc0fd44beb940ba2cbb0ca167741840595e7c96: <hi type="bold">Verse 10</hi> <div eID="gen17638" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen17639" type="x-p"/> Far be it from God - Rather, Wickedness, far be that from God; and from iniquity, the Almighty. The sense is sufficiently evident without the paraphrase in our version.
entries.7d581aa4f69fc74e558ef255423d849e41fa0de1: <hi type="bold">Verse 11</hi> <div eID="gen17639" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen17640" type="x-p"/> For the work of a man shall he render - God ever will do justice; the righteous shall never be forsaken, nor shall the wicked ultimately prosper.
entries.11f6177f7d323d42c6a30171f7c04c513ec27d04: <hi type="bold">Verse 13</hi> <div eID="gen17640" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen17641" type="x-p"/> Who hath given him a charge - Who is it that governs the world? Is it not God? Who disposes of all things in it? Is it not the Almighty, by his just and merciful providence? The government of the world shows the care, the justice, and the mercy of God.
entries.553d4c4bf86ca096004ee1de4c2192408f494526: <hi type="bold">Verse 14</hi> <div eID="gen17641" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen17642" type="x-p"/> If he set his heart upon man - I think this and the following verse should be read thus: - "If he set his heart upon man, he will gather his soul and breath to himself; for all flesh shall perish together, and man shall turn again unto dust." On whomsoever God sets his heart, that is, his love, though his body shall perish and turn to dust, like the rest of men, yet his soul will God gather to himself.
entries.9ec73d7cc1f142177b2e9d78cc4ac3c34908215e: <hi type="bold">Verse 17</hi> <div eID="gen17642" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen17643" type="x-p"/> Shall - he that hateth right govern? - Or, Shall he who hateth judgment, lie under obligation? It is preposterous to suppose that he who lives by no rule, should impose rules upon others. God, who is the fountain of all justice and righteousness, binds man by his laws; and wilt thou, therefore, pretend to condemn him who is the sum of righteousness?
entries.87aa934776162b3133efdb5db7ab075a4daf386a: <hi type="bold">Verse 18</hi> <div eID="gen17643" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen17644" type="x-p"/> Is it fit to say to a king, Thou art wicked? - The sentence is very short, and is thus translated by the Vulgate: Qui dicit regi, Apostata? Qui vocat duces impios? "Who says to a king, Apostate? Who calls leaders impious?" Literally, Who calls a king Belial? Who calls princes wicked? Civil governors should be treated with respect; no man should speak evil of the ruler of the people. This should never be permitted. Even where the man cannot be respected, because his moral conduct is improper, even there the office is sacred, and should be reverenced. He who permits himself to talk against the man, would destroy the office and authority, if he could.
entries.016ac93c94e455606ecf52422b765e4fa06a623b: <hi type="bold">Verse 19</hi> <div eID="gen17644" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen17645" type="x-p"/> That accepteth not - If it be utterly improper to speak against a king or civil governor, how much more so to speak disrespectfully of God, who is not influenced by human caprices or considerations, and who regards the rich and the poor alike, being equally his creatures, and equally dependent on his providence and mercy for their support and salvation.
entries.e11324d13e0baa51e9b42234969d0cbe8327467f: <hi type="bold">Verse 20</hi> <div eID="gen17645" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen17646" type="x-p"/> In a moment shall they die - Both are equally dependent on the Almighty for their breath and being; the mighty as well as the poor. If the great men of the earth have abused their power, he sometimes cuts them off by the most sudden and unexpected death; and even at midnight, when in security, and least capable of defense, they are cut off by the people whom they have oppressed, or by the invisible hand of the angel of death. This appears to be spoken in reference to Eastern tyrants, who seldom die a natural death.
entries.6348274bbaca527df64abf54e9d57e0da1dd73a7: <hi type="bold">Verse 22</hi> <div eID="gen17646" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen17647" type="x-p"/> There is no darkness - In this life; and no shadow of death in the other world - no annihilation in which the workers of iniquity may hide themselves, or take refuge.
entries.84d064f7d338dcba8e7905c6fc30320bab600a5c: <hi type="bold">Verse 23</hi> <div eID="gen17647" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen17648" type="x-p"/> For he will not lay upon man - The meaning appears to be this: He will not call man a second time into judgment; he does not try a cause twice; his decisions are just, and his sentence without appeal. Mr. Good translates: - "Behold, not to man hath he intrusted the time <div eID="gen17648" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen17649" type="x-p"/> Of coming into judgment with God." <div eID="gen17649" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen17650" type="x-p"/> Man's time is not in his own hand; nor is his lot cast or ruled by his own wisdom and power. When God thinks best, he will judge for him; and, if oppressed or calumniated, he will bring forth his righteousness as the light, and do him justice on his adversaries.
entries.cb14c334e5364edc8c79091fd104e9190905a7dd: <hi type="bold">Verse 24</hi> <div eID="gen17650" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen17651" type="x-p"/> He shall break in pieces - In multitudes of cases God depresses the proud, and raises up the humble and meek. Neither their strength nor number can afford them security.
entries.9a8bc4934f055ecd849e1824bda74dcff2f58461: <hi type="bold">Verse 25</hi> <div eID="gen17651" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen17652" type="x-p"/> He knoweth their works - He knows what they have done, and what they are plotting to do. <div eID="gen17652" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen17653" type="x-p"/> He overturneth them in the night - In the revolution of a single night the plenitude of power on which the day closed is annihilated. See the cases of Belshazzar and Babylon.
entries.512c31bdd648fb41feebc5cc1c8f36713d6fa705: <hi type="bold">Verse 26</hi> <div eID="gen17653" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen17654" type="x-p"/> He striketh them as wicked men - At other times he executes his judgments more openly; and they are suddenly destroyed in the sight of the people.
entries.e007de616c30bfad093595331ac6911bae059d84: <hi type="bold">Verse 27</hi> <div eID="gen17654" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen17655" type="x-p"/> Because they turned back - This is the reason why he has dealt with them in judgment. They had departed from him in their hearts, their moral conduct, and their civil government. He is speaking of corrupt and tyrannical rulers. And they did not, would not, understand any of his ways.
entries.7d5a8c11630db54ba16977b89cd3942fe52df773: <hi type="bold">Verse 28</hi> <div eID="gen17655" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen17656" type="x-p"/> So that they cause the cry of the poor - They were cruel and oppressive: the poor cried through their distresses, and against their oppressors; and God heard the cry of the poor. Nothing so dreadful appears in the court of heaven against an unfeeling, hardhearted, and cruel man of power, as the prayers, tears, and groans of the poor. In times of little liberality, when some men thought they did God service by persecuting those who did not exactly receive their creed, nor worship God in their way, a certain great man in Scotland grievously persecuted his tenants, because they had religious meetings in private houses out of the order of the establishment; though he never molested them when they spent their time and their money in the alehouse. A holy, simple woman, one of those people, went one morning to the house of the great persecutor, and desired to speak with him. The servant desired to know her message, and he would deliver it; for she could not be admitted. She told him she could deliver her message to none but his master; said it was a matter of great importance, and concerned himself intimately, and alone. The servant having delivered this message, and stated that the woman appeared to have something particular on her mind, his worship condescended to see her. "What is your business with me?" said he, in a haughty, overbearing tone. To which she answered, "Sir, we are a hantle o' puir folk at - , who are strivin' to sairve God accordin' to our ain conscience, and to get our sauls sav'd: yee persecute us; and I am come to beg yee to let us alane, and in ye dinna, we'll pray yee dead." This rhetoric was irresistible. His lordship did not know what influence such people might have in heaven; he did not like to put such prayers to the proof; wisely took the old woman's advice, and e'en let them alane. He was safe; they were satisfied; and God had the glory. When the poor refer their cause to God, he is a terrible avenger. Let the potsherds strive with the potsherds of the earth; but wo to the man that contendeth with his Maker.
entries.cba1131d37302585415a4841505feb65fddedbdd: <hi type="bold">Verse 29</hi> <div eID="gen17656" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen17657" type="x-p"/> When he giveth quietness, who then can make trouble? - How beautiful is this sentiment, and how true! He ever acts as a sovereign, but his actions are all wise and just. If he give quietness, who dares to give trouble? And if he give to every human being the right to worship himself according to their conscience, for the director of which he gives both his word and his Spirit, who shall dare to say to another, "Thou shalt worship God in my way, or not at all;" or, through a pretended liberality, say, "Thou shalt be tolerated to worship him so and so;" and even that toleration be shackled and limited? Reader, thou hast as much right to tolerate another's mode of worship as he has to tolerate thine: or, in other words, neither of you have any such right at all; the pretension is as absurd as it is wicked. If, however, there be any thing in the religious practice of any particular people that is inimical, by fair construction, to the peace of the country, then the civil power may interfere, as they ought to do in all cases of insurrection; but let no such inference be drawn when not most obviously flowing from the practice of the people, and the principles they profess; and when solemnly disclaimed by the persons in question. Whatever converts sinners from the error of their ways must be good to society and profitable to the state. <div eID="gen17657" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen17658" type="x-p"/> Whether it be done against a nation - He defends and supports nations or individuals howsoever weak, against their enemies, howsoever numerous and powerful. He destroys nations or individuals who have filled up the measure of their political or moral iniquity, though all other nations and individuals stand up in their support.
entries.24b586817cecef27aa0e04594b3f40eacf1b44a9: <hi type="bold">Verse 30</hi> <div eID="gen17658" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen17659" type="x-p"/> That the hypocrite reign not - The Vulgate translates, Who causes a wicked man to reign because of the sins of the people. This was precisely the defense which Hegiage, the oppressive ruler of the Babylonian Irak, under the caliph Abdul Malec, made when he found the people in a state of insurrection. See at the end of the chapter, <reference osisRef="Job.34.37">Job 34:37</reference> (note).
entries.f7051daed0a70592df18ce52e372066e48794c6a: <hi type="bold">Verse 31</hi> <div eID="gen17659" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen17660" type="x-p"/> Surely it is meet to be said unto God - This is Elihu's exhortation to Job: Humble thyself before God, and say, "I have suffered - I will not offend."
entries.11447d72da9f6714b5ddf441a1b9885a62bb7b47: <hi type="bold">Verse 32</hi> <div eID="gen17660" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen17661" type="x-p"/> That which I see not - "What I do not know, teach thou me; wherein I have done iniquity, I will do so no more."
entries.94991012adad1336701ec9e10ef9fa5d2d5c2eff: <hi type="bold">Verse 33</hi> <div eID="gen17661" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen17662" type="x-p"/> According to thy mind? he will recompense it - Mr. Good renders the whole passage thus: - "Then in the presence of thy tribes <div eID="gen17662" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen17663" type="x-p"/> According as thou art bruised shall he make it whole. <div eID="gen17663" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen17664" type="x-p"/> But it is thine to choose, and not mine; <div eID="gen17664" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen17665" type="x-p"/> So, what thou determinest, say." <div eID="gen17665" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen17666" type="x-p"/> This may at least be considered a paraphrase on the very obscure original. If thou wilt not thus come unto him, he will act according to justice, whether that be for or against thee. Choose what part thou wilt take, to humble thyself under the mighty hand of God, or still persist in thy supposed integrity. Speak, therefore; the matter concerns thee, not me; but let me know what thou art determined to do.
entries.278776afa3e565b9234b0809cf1826884492bea8: <hi type="bold">Verse 34</hi> <div eID="gen17666" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen17667" type="x-p"/> Let men of understanding tell me - I wish to converse with wise men; and by men of wisdom I wish what I have said to be judged.
entries.00e3a2ca13517ce10ffd04daa98ec53754101091: <hi type="bold">Verse 35</hi> <div eID="gen17667" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen17668" type="x-p"/> Job hath spoken without knowledge - There is no good in arguing with a self-willed, self-conceited man. Job has spoken like a man destitute of wisdom and discretion.
entries.f7de885861610274c6b1e45b50dac327b8ff0792: <hi type="bold">Verse 36</hi> <div eID="gen17668" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen17669" type="x-p"/> My desire is that Job may be tried unto the end - אבי יבחן איוב abi yibbachen Aiyob, "My father, let Job be tried." So the Vulgate, Pater mi, probetur Job. But it may be as in the common translation, I wish Job to be tried; or, as Mr. Good renders it, Verily, let Job be pursued to conquest for replying like wicked men. This is a very harsh wish: but the whole chapter is in the same spirit; nearly destitute of mildness and compassion. Who could suppose that such arguings could come out of the mouth of the loving Savior of mankind? The reader will recollect that a very pious divine has supposed Elihu to be Jesus Christ!
entries.ee147fcc7fabee8731cf3ed91eba97614a1c9cde: <hi type="bold">Verse 37</hi> <div eID="gen17669" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen17670" type="x-p"/> He addeth rebellion unto his sin - An ill-natured, cruel, and unfounded assertion, borne out by nothing which Job had ever said or intended; and indeed, more severe than the most inveterate of his friends (so called) had ever spoken. Mr. Good makes this virulent conclusion still more virulent and uncharitable, by translating thus: - "For he would add to his transgressions apostasy; <div eID="gen17670" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen17671" type="x-p"/> He would clap his hands in the midst of us: <div eID="gen17671" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen17672" type="x-p"/> Yea, he would tempest his words up to God." <div eID="gen17672" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen17673" type="x-p"/> There was no need of adding a caustic here; the words in the tamest translation are tart enough. Though Elihu began well and tolerantly, he soon got into the spirit, and under the mistake, of those who had preceded him in this "tempest of words." <div eID="gen17673" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen17674" type="x-p"/> On <reference osisRef="Job.34.30">Job 34:30</reference> I have referred to the case of Hegiage, governor of the Babylonian Irak, under the caliph Abdul Malec. When Hegiage was informed that the people were in a state of mutiny because of his oppressive government, before they broke out into open acts of hostility, he mounted on an eminence, and thus harangued them: - "God has given me dominion over you; if I exercise it with severity, think not that by putting me to death your condition will be mended. From the manner in which you live you must be always ill-treated, for God has many executors of his justice; and when I am dead he will send you another, who will probably execute his orders against you with more rigour. Do you wish your prince to be moderate and merciful? Then exercise righteousness, and be obedient to the laws. Consider that your own conduct is the cause of the good or evil treatment which you receive from him. A prince may be compared to a mirror; all that you see in him is the reflection of the objects which you present before him." The people immediately dropped their weapons, and quietly returned to their respective avocations. This man was one of the most valiant, eloquent, and cruel rulers of his time; he lived towards the close of the 7th century of the Christian era. He is said to have put to death 120,000 people; and to have had 50,000 in his prisons at the time of his decease. Yet this man was capable of generous actions. The following anecdote is given by the celebrated Persian poet Jami, in his Baharistan: - Hegiage, having been separated from his attendants one day in the chase, came to a place where he found an Arab feeding his camels. The camels starting at his sudden approach, the Arab lifted up his head, and seeing a man splendidly arrayed, became incensed, and said, Who is this who with his fine clothes comes into the desert to frighten my camels? The curse of Good light upon him! The governor, approaching the Arab, saluted him very civilly, with the salaam, Peace be unto thee! The Arab, far from returning the salutation, said, I wish thee neither peace, nor any other blessing of God. Hegiage, without seeming to heed what he had said, asked him very civilly "to give him a little water to drink." The Arab in a surly tone, answered, If thou desirest to drink, take the pains to alight, and draw for thyself; for I am neither thy companion nor thy slave. The governor accordingly alighted, and having drank, asked the Arab, "Whom dost thou think the greatest and most excellent of men?" The prophet sent by God, said the Arab, and thou mayest burst with spleen. "And what thinkest thou of Aaly?" returned Hegiage. No tongue can declare his excellence, said the Arab. "What," asked Hegiage, "is thy opinion of the caliph Abdul Malec?" I believe him to be a very bad prince, replied the Arab. "For what reason?" said Hegiage. Because, said the Arab, he hath sent us for governor the most execrable wretch under heaven. Hegiage, finding himself thus characterized, was silent; but his attendants coming up, he rejoined them, and ordered them to bring the Arab with them. The next day Hegiage ordered him to be set at table with himself, and bade him "eat freely." The Arab, ere he tasted, said his usual grace, "God grant that the end of this repast may be no worse than the beginning!" While at meat the governor asked him, "Dost thou recollect the discourse we had together yesterday?" The Arab replied, God prosper thee in all things! but as to the secret of yesterday, take heed that thou disclose it not to-day. "I will not," said Hegiage; "but thou must choose one of these two things; either acknowledge me for thy master, and I will retain thee about my person; or else I will send thee to Abdul Malec, and tell him what thou hast said of him." There is a third course, replied the Arab, preferable to those two. "Well, what is that?" said the governor. Why, send me back to the desert, and pray God that we may never see each other's face again. Cruel and vindictive as Hegiage was, he could not help being pleased with the frankness and courage of the man; and not only forgave him the preceding insults but ordered him 10,000 pieces of silver, and sent him back to the desert, according to his wish.  <chapter eID="Job.34"/> <div eID="gen17674" type="x-p"/>

entries.cfeddad49effe4f02602f01b98ffa8145ba9a349: <reference osisRef="Job.34.1-Job.4.1">Job 34:1-4   1</reference>  Then began Elihu and said:   2  Hear, ye wise men, my words, <div eID="gen8413" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen8414" type="x-p"/> And ye experienced ones, give ear to me!   3  For the ear trieth words, <div eID="gen8414" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen8415" type="x-p"/> As the palate tasteth by eating.   4  Let us find out what is right, <div eID="gen8415" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen8416" type="x-p"/> Let us explore among ourselves what is good. <div eID="gen8416" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen8417" type="x-p"/> After his first speech Elihu has made a brief pause; now since Job is silent, he begins anew. ויען ויאמר, lxx correctly, here as in all other instances where the phrase occurs: ὑπολαβὼν λέγει, taking up the word he said. The wise and the knowing (Arab. <hi type="italic">‛ulamâ</hi>), whose attention he bespeaks, are not Job and the three (Umbr., Hahn), who are indeed a party, and as such a subject for the arbitrative appearance of Elihu; also not every one capable of forming a judgment (Hirz.); but those in the circle of spectators and listeners which, as is assumed, has assembled round the disputants (Schlottm.). In <reference osisRef="Job.33.4">Job 33:4</reference> Elihu does not expressly mean his own ear, but that of the persons addressed: he establishes his summons to prove what he says by the general thought brought over from <reference osisRef="Job.12.11">Job 12:11</reference>, and as there (comp. <reference osisRef="Job.5.7">Job 5:7</reference>; <reference osisRef="Job.11.12">Job 11:12</reference>), clothed in the form of the emblematic proverb, - that as there is a bodily, so there is also a mental organ of sense which tries its perceptions. לאכל is not intended as expressing a purpose (<hi type="italic">ad vescendum</hi>), but as a gerundive (<hi type="italic">vescendo</hi>). The phrase בּחר משׁפּט, occurring only here, signifies neither to institute a search for the purpose of decision (Schult. and others), since בחר does not signify to decide upon anything, nor to investigate a cause (Hahn), which would be נבחנה, but to test and choose what is right, δοκιμάζειν καὶ τὸ καλὸν κατέχειν, <reference osisRef="1Thess.5.21">1Th 5:21</reference>, after which the parallel runs: <hi type="italic">cognoscamus inter nos</hi> (i.e., in common) <hi type="italic">quid bonum.</hi>
entries.e2b278a4f124e65e250394d223fe0c23916c6044: <reference osisRef="Job.34.5-Job.9.5">Job 34:5-9   5</reference>  For Job hath said: “I am guiltless, “And God hath put aside my right.   6  “Shall I lie in spite of my right, “Incurable is mine arrow without transgression.”   7  Where is there a man like Job, <div eID="gen8417" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen8418" type="x-p"/> Who drinketh scorning like water,   8  And keepeth company with the workers of iniquity, <div eID="gen8418" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen8419" type="x-p"/> And walketh with wicked men,   9  So that he saith: “A man hath no profit “From entering into fellowship with God”?! <div eID="gen8419" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen8420" type="x-p"/> That in relation to God, thinking of Him as a punishing judge, he is righteous or in the right, i.e., guiltless (צדקתּי with <hi type="italic">Pathach</hi> in pause, according to Ew. §93, <hi type="italic">c,</hi> from צדק = צדק, but perhaps, comp. <reference osisRef="Prov.24.30">Pro 24:30</reference>; <reference osisRef="Ps.102.26">Psa 102:26</reference>, because the <hi type="italic">Athnach</hi> is taken only as of the value of <hi type="italic">Zakeph</hi>), Job has said <hi type="italic">verbatim</hi> in <reference osisRef="Job.13.18">Job 13:18</reference>, and according to meaning, <reference osisRef="Job.23.10">Job 23:10</reference>; <reference osisRef="Job.27.7">Job 27:7</reference>, and throughout; that He puts aside his right (the right of the guiltless, and therefore not of one coming under punishment): Job 27:2. That in spite of his right (על, to be interpreted, according to Schultens’ example, just like <reference osisRef="Job.10.7">Job 10:7</reference>; <reference osisRef="Job.16.17">Job 16:17</reference>), i.e., although right is on his side, yet he must be accounted a liar, since his own testimony is belied by the wrathful form of his affliction, that therefore the appearance of wrong remains inalienably attached to him, we find in idea in <reference osisRef="Job.9.20">Job 9:20</reference> and freq. Elihu makes Job call his affliction חצּי, i.e., an arrow sticking in him, viz., the arrow of the wrath of God (on the objective <hi type="italic">suff</hi>. comp. on <reference osisRef="Job.23.2">Job 23:2</reference>), after <reference osisRef="Job.6.4">Job 6:4</reference>; <reference osisRef="Job.16.9">Job 16:9</reference>; <reference osisRef="Job.19.11">Job 19:11</reference>; and that this his arrow, i.e., the pain which it causes him, is incurably bad, desperately malignant without (בּלי as <reference osisRef="Job.8.11">Job 8:11</reference>) פּשׁע, i.e., sins existing as the ground of it, from which he would be obliged to suppose they had thrust him out of the condition of favour, is Job’s constant complaint (vid., e.g., Job 13:23.). Another utterance of Job closely connected with it has so roused Elihu’s indignation, that he prefaces it with the exclamation of astonishment: Who is a man like Job, i.e., where in all the world (מי as <reference osisRef="2Sam.7.23">2Sa 7:23</reference>) has this Job his equal, who ... . The attributive clause refers to Job; “to drink scorn (here: blasphemy) like water,” is, according to <reference osisRef="Job.15.16">Job 15:16</reference>, equivalent to to give one’s self up to mockery with delight, and to find satisfaction in it. ארח לחברה, to go over to any one’s side, looks like a poeticized prose expression. ללכת is a continuation of the ארח, according to Ew. §351, <hi type="italic">c</hi>, but not directly in the sense "and he goes,” but, as in the similar examples, <reference osisRef="Jer.17.10">Jer 17:10</reference>; <reference osisRef="Jer.44.19">Jer 44:19</reference>; <reference osisRef="2Chr.7.17">2Ch 7:17</reference>, and freq., in the sense of: “he is in the act of going;” comp. on <reference osisRef="Job.36.20">Job 36:20</reference> and Hab 1:17. The utterance runs: a man does not profit, viz., himself (on the use of סכן of persons as well as of things, vid., on <reference osisRef="Job.22.2">Job 22:2</reference>), by his having joyous and familiar intercourse (בּרצתו, as little equivalent to בּרוּץ as in <reference osisRef="Ps.50.18">Psa 50:18</reference>) with God. Job has nowhere expressly said this, but certainly the declaration in <reference osisRef="Job.9.22">Job 9:22</reference>, in connection with the repeated complaints concerning the anomalous distribution of human destinies (vid., especially <reference osisRef="Job.21.7">Job 21:7</reference>, <reference osisRef="Job.24.1">Job 24:1</reference>), are the premises for such a conclusion. That Elihu, in <reference osisRef="Job.34.7">Job 34:7</reference>, is more harsh against Job than the friends ever were (comp. e.g., the well-measured reproach of Eliphaz, <reference osisRef="Job.15.4">Job 15:4</reference>), and that he puts words into Job’s moth which occur nowhere <hi type="italic">verbatim</hi> in his speeches, is worked up by the Latin fathers (Jer., Philippus Presbyter, Beda,<note placement="foot">Philippus Presbyter was a disciple of Jerome. His <hi type="italic">Comm. in Iobum</hi> is extant in many forms, partly epitomized, partly interpolated (on this subject, vid., <hi type="italic">Hieronymi Opp. ed. Vallarsi,</hi> iii. 895ff.). The commentary of Beda, dedicated to a certain Nectarius (Vecterius), is fundamentally that of this Philippus.</note> <div eID="gen8420" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen8421" type="x-p"/> Gregory) in favour of their unfavourable judgment of Elihu; the Greek fathers, however, are deprived of all opportunity of understanding him by the translation of the lxx (in which μυκτηρισμόν signifies the scorn of others which Job must swallow down, comp. <reference osisRef="Prov.26.6">Pro 26:6</reference>), which here perverts everything.
entries.8debbd5fd6a1ba8554a589bf6afd265b449bd264: <reference osisRef="Job.34.10-Job.11.10">Job 34:10-11 10</reference>  Therefore, men of understanding, hearken to me! <div eID="gen8421" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen8422" type="x-p"/> Far be it from god to do evil, <div eID="gen8422" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen8423" type="x-p"/> And the Almighty to act wrongfully. 11  No indeed, man’s work He recompenseth to him, <div eID="gen8423" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen8424" type="x-p"/> And according to man’s walk He causeth it to be with him. “Men of heart,” according to <hi type="italic">Psychol</hi>. S. 249, comp. 254, is equivalent to noee'mones or noeeroi' (lxx συνετοὶ καρδίας). The clause which Elihu makes prominent in the following reply is the very axiom which the three defend, perfectly true in itself, but falsely applied by them: evil, wrong, are inconceivable on the part of God; instead of וּלשׁדּי it is only ושׁדּי in the second member of the verse, with the omission of the <hi type="italic">praep</hi>. - a frequent form of ellipsis, particularly in Isaiah (<reference osisRef="Isa.15.8">Isa 15:8</reference>; <reference osisRef="Isa.28.6">Isa 28:6</reference>; <reference osisRef="Isa.48.14">Isa 48:14</reference>; <reference osisRef="Isa.61.7">Isa 61:7</reference>, comp. <reference osisRef="Ezek.25.15">Eze 25:15</reference>). Far removed from acting wickedly and wrongfully, on the contrary He practises recompense exactly apportioned to man’s deeds, and ever according to the walk of each one (ארח like דּרך or דּרכי, e.g., <reference osisRef="Jer.32.19">Jer 32:19</reference>, in an ethical sense) He causes it to overtake him, i.e., to happen to him (המציא only here and <reference osisRef="Job.37.13">Job 37:13</reference>). The general assertion brought forward against Job is now proved.
entries.863c87b9732d33fbffe0b8523baf01513fd63073: <reference osisRef="Job.34.12-Job.15.12">Job 34:12-15 12</reference>  Yea verily God acteth not wickedly, <div eID="gen8424" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen8425" type="x-p"/> And the Almighty perverteth not the right. 13  Who hath given the earth in charge to Him? <div eID="gen8425" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen8426" type="x-p"/> And who hath disposed the whole globe? 14  If He only set His heart upon Himself, <div eID="gen8426" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen8427" type="x-p"/> If He took back His breath and His inspiration to Himself: 15  All flesh would expire together, <div eID="gen8427" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen8428" type="x-p"/> And man would return to dust. <div eID="gen8428" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen8429" type="x-p"/> With אף אמנם (Yea verily, as <reference osisRef="Job.19.4">Job 19:4</reference>, “and really”) the counter-assertion of <reference osisRef="Job.34.11">Job 34:11</reference> is repeated, but negatively expressed (comp. <reference osisRef="Job.8.3">Job 8:3</reference>). הרשׁיע signifies sometimes to act as רשׁע, and at others to be set forth and condemned as a רשׁע; here, as the connection requires, it is the former. <reference osisRef="Job.34.13">Job 34:13</reference> begins the proof. Ewald’s interpretation: who searcheth, and Hahn's: who careth for the earth beside Him, are hazardous and unnecessary. פּקד with על of the person and the acc. of the thing signifies: to enjoin anything as a duty on any one, to entrust anything to any one, <reference osisRef="Job.36.23">Job 36:23</reference>; Num 4:27; <reference osisRef="2Chr.36.23">2Ch 36:23</reference>; therefore: who has made the earth, i.e., the care of it, a duty to Him? ארצה (<hi type="italic">Milel</hi>) is not to be refined into the meaning “to the earth” (as here by Schultens and a few others, <reference osisRef="Isa.9.1">Isa 9:1</reference> by Luzzatto: he hath smitten down, better: dishonoured, to the earth with a light stroke), but is poetically equivalent to ארץ, as לילה (comp. modern Greek ἡ νύχθα) is in prose equivalent to ליל. <hi type="italic"><reference osisRef="Job.34.13">Job 34:13</reference></hi> is by no means, with Ew. and Hahn, to be translated: who observes (considers) the whole globe, שׂים as <reference osisRef="Job.34.23">Job 34:23</reference>; <reference osisRef="Job.4.20">Job 4:20</reference>; <reference osisRef="Job.24.12">Job 24:12</reference> - the expression would be too contracted to affirm that no one but God bestowed providential attention upon the earth; and if we have understood <hi type="italic"><reference osisRef="Job.34.13">Job 34:13</reference></hi> correctly, the thought is also inappropriate. A more appropriate thought is gained, if עליו is supplied from <hi type="italic"><reference osisRef="Job.34.13">Job 34:13</reference></hi>: who has enjoined upon Him the whole circle of the earth (Saad., Gecat., Hirz., Schlottm.); but this continued force of the עליו into the second independent question is improbable in connection with the repetition of מי. Therefore: who has appointed, i.e., established (שׂם as <reference osisRef="Job.38.5">Job 38:5</reference>; <reference osisRef="Isa.44.7">Isa 44:7</reference>), - a still somewhat more suitable thought, going logically further, since the one giving the charge ought to be the lord of him who receives the commission, and therefore the Creator of the world. This is just God alone, by whose רוּח and נשׁמה the animal world as well as the world of men (vid., <reference osisRef="Job.32.8">Job 32:8</reference>; <reference osisRef="Job.33.4">Job 33:4</reference>) has its life, <reference osisRef="Job.34.14">Job 34:14</reference> : if He should direct His heart, i.e., His attention (שׂים לב אל, as <reference osisRef="Job.2.3">Job 2:3</reference>), to Himself (emphatic: Himself alone), draw in (אסף as <reference osisRef="Ps.104.29">Psa 104:29</reference>; comp. for the matter <reference osisRef="Eccl.12.7">Ecc 12:7</reference>, <hi type="italic">Psychol</hi>. S. 406) to Himself His inspiration and breath (which emanated from Him or was effected by Him), all flesh would sink together, i.e., die off at once (this, as it appears, has reference to the taking back of the animal life, רוח), and man would return (this has reference to the taking back of the human spirit, נשׁמה) to dust (על instead of אל, perhaps with reference to the usual use of the על־עפר, <reference osisRef="Job.17.16">Job 17:16</reference>; <reference osisRef="Job.20.11">Job 20:11</reference>; <reference osisRef="Job.21.26">Job 21:26</reference>). <div eID="gen8429" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen8430" type="x-p"/> Only a few modern expositors refer אליו, as Targ. Jer. and Syr., to man instead of reflexively to God; the majority rightly decide in favour of the idea which even Grotius perceived: <hi type="italic">si sibi ipsi tantum bonus esse (sui unius curam habere) vellet</hi>. אם followed by the <hi type="italic">fut</hi>. signifies either <hi type="italic">si velit</hi> (lxx ει ̓ βούλοιτο), as here, or as more frequently, <hi type="italic">si vellet,</hi> <reference osisRef="Ps.50.12">Psa 50:12</reference>; <reference osisRef="Ps.139.8">Psa 139:8</reference>, Oba 1:4, <reference osisRef="Isa.10.22">Isa 10:22</reference>; <reference osisRef="Amos.9.2">Amo 9:2</reference>-4. It is worthy of remark that, according to Norzi’s statement, the Babylonian texts presented ישׁיב, <hi type="italic"><reference osisRef="Job.34.14">Job 34:14</reference></hi>, as <hi type="italic">Chethîb</hi>, ישׂים as <hi type="italic">Kerî</hi> (like our Palestine text, <reference osisRef="Dan.11.18">Dan 11:18</reference>), which a MS of De Rossi, with a Persian translation, confirms; the reading gives a fine idea: that God’s heart is turned towards the world, and is unclosed; its ethical condition of life would then be like its physical ground of life, that God’s spirit dwells in it; the drawing back of the heart, and the taking back to Himself of the spirit, would be equivalent to the exclusion of the world from God’s love and life. However, ישׂים implies the same; for a reference of God’s thinking and willing to Himself, with the exclusion of the world, would be just a removal of His love. Elihu’s proof is this: God does not act wrongly, for the government of the world is not a duty imposed upon Him from without, but a relation entered into freely by Him: the world is not the property of another, but of His free creative appointment; and how unselfishly, how devoid of self-seeking He governs it, is clear from the fact, that by the impartation of His living creative breath He sustains every living thing, and does not, as He easily might, allow them to fall away into nothingness. There is therefore a divine love which has called the world into being and keeps it in being; and this love, as the perfect opposite of sovereign caprice, is a pledge for the absolute righteousness of the divine rule.
entries.e471bbda5c2532a0ac59b7b4b1524967630cc101: <reference osisRef="Job.34.16-Job.20.16">Job 34:16-20 16</reference>  And oh understand now, hear this; <div eID="gen8430" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen8431" type="x-p"/> Hearken to the sound of my words. 17  Would one who hateth right also be able to subdue? <div eID="gen8431" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen8432" type="x-p"/> Or wilt thou condemn the All-just? 18  Is it becoming to say to a king: Worthless One!? <div eID="gen8432" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen8433" type="x-p"/> Thou evil-doer! to princes? 19  To Him who accepteth not the person of rulers, <div eID="gen8433" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen8434" type="x-p"/> And regardeth not the noble before the poor: <div eID="gen8434" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen8435" type="x-p"/> For they are all the work of His hands. 20  In a moment they die, and at midnight <div eID="gen8435" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen8436" type="x-p"/> The people are overthrown and perish, <div eID="gen8436" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen8437" type="x-p"/> And they put aside the mighty - not by the hand of man. <div eID="gen8437" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen8438" type="x-p"/> This strophe contains several grammatical rarities. At first sight it appears that <hi type="italic"><reference osisRef="Job.34.16">Job 34:16</reference></hi> ought to be translated: “and if there is understanding (viz., to thee = if thou hast), then hear this.” But בּינה is accented as <hi type="italic">Milel</hi> and with <hi type="italic">Mercha</hi>, and can therefore not be a substantive (Hirz., Hahn, and others); for the retreat of the accent would be absolutely incomprehensible, and instead of a conjunctive, a distinctive, viz., <hi type="italic">Dechî</hi>, ought to be expected. Several of the old expositors, therefore, interpret with Nolde: <hi type="italic">quod quum ita sit, intellige; </hi>but this elliptical ואם, well as it might also be used for <reference osisRef="Job.21.4">Job 21:4</reference>, is unsupportable; the <hi type="italic">Makkeph</hi> between the two words is also against it, which rather arises from the assumption that בּינה is the <hi type="italic">imperat.,</hi> and אם as an exception, like <reference osisRef="Gen.23.13">Gen 23:13</reference>, is an optative particle joined to the <hi type="italic">imper</hi>. 2 instead of to the <hi type="italic">fut.:</hi> “and if thou shouldst observe” (= ואם־תּבין). To translate <hi type="italic"><reference osisRef="Job.34.17">Job 34:17</reference></hi> with Schultens: <hi type="italic">num iram osor judicii frenabit,</hi> is impracticable on account of the order of the words, and gives a thought that is inappropriate here. אף is a particle, and the <hi type="italic">fut</hi>. is <hi type="italic">potentialis:</hi> is it also possible that an enemy of right should govern? (חבשׁ, <hi type="italic">imperio coercere,</hi> as אצר   <reference osisRef="1Sam.9.17">1Sa 9:17</reference>, אסר <reference osisRef="Ps.105.22">Psa 105:22</reference>); right and government are indeed mutually conditioned, without right everything would fall into anarchy and confusion. In <hi type="italic"><reference osisRef="Job.34.17">Job 34:17</reference></hi> this is applied to the Ruler of the world: or (ואם, <hi type="italic">an</hi>, as <reference osisRef="Job.8.3">Job 8:3</reference>; <reference osisRef="Job.21.4">Job 21:4</reference>; <reference osisRef="Job.40.9">Job 40:9</reference>) wilt thou condemn the mighty just One, i.e., the All-just? As Elihu calls God שׂגּיא כח, <reference osisRef="Job.37.23">Job 37:23</reference>, as the Almighty, and as the Omniscient One, תּמים דּעים, <reference osisRef="Job.37.16">Job 37:16</reference>, so here as the All-just One, צדּיק כּבּיר. The two adjectives are put side by side ἀσυνδέτως, as is frequently the case in Arabic, and form one compound idea, Ew. §270, <hi type="italic">d</hi>.
entries.36db1ecfae1a651e4216859ccad1221cae97b665: Job 34:21-23 21  For His eyes are upon the ways of each one, <div eID="gen8440" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen8441" type="x-p"/> And He seeth all his steps. 22  There is no darkness nor shadow of death <div eID="gen8441" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen8442" type="x-p"/> Wherein the workers of iniquity might hide themselves. 23  For He needeth not long to regard a man <div eID="gen8442" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen8443" type="x-p"/> That he may enter into judgment with God. <div eID="gen8443" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen8444" type="x-p"/> As the preceding strophe showed that God’s creative order excludes all partiality, so this strophe shows that His omniscience qualifies Him to be an impartial judge. He sees everything, nothing can escape His gaze; He sees through man without being obliged to wait for the result of a judicial investigation. שׂים with על does not here signify: to lay upon (Saad., Gecat.), but as <reference osisRef="Job.37.15">Job 37:15</reference>, and as with אל (<reference osisRef="Job.34.14">Job 34:14</reference>) or בּ (<reference osisRef="Job.23.6">Job 23:6</reference>); to direct one’s attention (supply לבּו, <reference osisRef="Job.1.8">Job 1:8</reference>) towards anything; the <hi type="italic">fut</hi>. has here a modal signification; עוד is used as e.g., <reference osisRef="Gen.46.29">Gen 46:29</reference> : again and again, continuously; and in the clause expressive of purpose it is אל־אל (instead of אליו, a very favourite combination used throughout the whole book, <reference osisRef="Job.5.8">Job 5:8</reference>; <reference osisRef="Job.8.5">Job 8:5</reference>; <reference osisRef="Job.13.3">Job 13:3</reference>, and so on) from the human standpoint: He, the all-seeing One, needs not to observe him long that he should enter into judgment with God - He knows him thoroughly before any investigation takes place, which is not said without allusion to Job’s vehement longing to be able to appear before God’s tribunal.
entries.50323d792ef353aac33bf85109fe60a1fc0b0d6a: <reference osisRef="Job.34.24-Job.28.24">Job 34:24-28 24</reference>  He breaketh the mighty in pieces without investigation <div eID="gen8444" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen8445" type="x-p"/> And setteth others in their place. 25  Thus He seeth through their works, <div eID="gen8445" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen8446" type="x-p"/> And causeth their overthrow by night, thus they are crushed. 26  He smiteth them after the manner of evil-doers <div eID="gen8446" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen8447" type="x-p"/> In the sight of the public. 27  For for such purpose are they fallen away from Him <div eID="gen8447" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen8448" type="x-p"/> And have not considered any of His ways, 28  To cause the cry of the poor to come up to Him, <div eID="gen8448" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen8449" type="x-p"/> And that He should hear the cry of the needy. <div eID="gen8449" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen8450" type="x-p"/> He makes short work (לא־חקר for בּלא, as <reference osisRef="Job.12.24">Job 12:24</reference>; <reference osisRef="Job.38.26">Job 38:26</reference> : without research, viz., into their conduct, which is at once manifest to Him; not: in an incomprehensible manner, which is unsuitable, and still less: <hi type="italic">innumerabiles</hi>, as Jer., Syr.) with the mighty (כּבּירים, Arab. <hi type="italic">kibâr , kubarâ</hi>), and in consequence of this (<hi type="italic">fut. consec.</hi>) sets up (<hi type="italic">constituit</hi>) others, i.e., better and worthier rulers (comp. אהר, <reference osisRef="Job.8.19">Job 8:19</reference>; <reference osisRef="Isa.55.1-Isa.13.15">Isa 55:1-13 :15</reference>), in their stead. The following לכן is not equivalent to לכן אשׁר, for which no satisfactory instance exists; on the contrary, לכן here, as more frequently, introduces not the real consequence (<reference osisRef="Job.20.2">Job 20:2</reference>), but a logical inference, something that directly follows in and with what precedes (corresponding to the Greek ἄρα, just so, consequently), comp. <reference osisRef="Job.42.3">Job 42:3</reference>; <reference osisRef="Isa.26.14">Isa 26:14</reference>; <reference osisRef="Isa.61.7">Isa 61:7</reference>; <reference osisRef="Jer.2.33">Jer 2:33</reference>; <reference osisRef="Jer.5.2">Jer 5:2</reference>; Zec 11:7 (vid., Köhler <hi type="italic">in loc.</hi>). Thus, then, as He hereby proves, He is thoroughly acquainted with their actions (מעבּד, nowhere besides in the book of Job, an Aramaizing expression for מעשׂה). This abiding fact of divine omniscience, inferred from the previously-mentioned facts, then serves again in its turn, in <hi type="italic"><reference osisRef="Job.34.25">Job 34:25</reference></hi>, as the source of facts by which it is verified. לילה is by no means an obj. The expositions: <hi type="italic">et inducit noctem </hi>(Jer.), He walks in the night in which He has veiled Himself (Umbr.), <hi type="italic">convertit eos in noctem</hi> (Syr., Arab.), and such like, all read in the two words what they do not imply. It is either to be translated: He throws them by night (לילה as <reference osisRef="Job.27.20">Job 27:20</reference>) upon the heaps (הפך as <reference osisRef="Prov.12.7">Pro 12:7</reference>), or, since the verb has no objective <hi type="italic">suff.:</hi> He maketh a reformation or overthrow during the night, i.e., creates during the night a new order of things, and they who stood at the head of the former affairs are crushed by the catastrophe.
entries.893099354b108d52be70cee7dc24b6bb1b10c704: Job 34:29-32 29  If He, however, maketh peace, who will then condemn? <div eID="gen8451" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen8452" type="x-p"/> And if He hideth His countenance - who then can behold Him? - <div eID="gen8452" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen8453" type="x-p"/> Both concerning numbers and individuals together: 30  That godless men reign not, <div eID="gen8453" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen8454" type="x-p"/> That they be not nets to the people. 31  For one, indeed, saith to God, “I have been proud, I will not do evil; 32  “What I see not, show Thou me; “If I have done wrong, I will do it no more”!? - <div eID="gen8454" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen8455" type="x-p"/> If God makes peace (ישׁקיט as <reference osisRef="Ps.94.13">Psa 94:13</reference>, comp. <reference osisRef="Isa.14.7">Isa 14:7</reference>, הארץ שׁקטה כל־, viz., after the overthrow of the tyrant) in connection with such crying oppression of the poor, who will then condemn Him without the rather recognising therein His comprehensive justice? The conjecture ירעשׁ<note placement="foot">Vid., Grätz in Frankel’s <hi type="italic">Monatsschrift</hi>, 1861, i.</note> is not required either here or <reference osisRef="1Sam.14.47">1Sa 14:47</reference> (where הרשׁיע signifies to punish the guilty); ירשׁע is also not to be translated <hi type="italic">turbabit</hi> (Rosenm.), since רשׁע (Arab. <hi type="italic">rs‛ , rsg</hi>) according to its primitive notion does not signify “to be restless, to rage,” but “to be relaxed, hollow” (opposite of צדק, Arab. <hi type="italic">ṣdq</hi>, to be hard, firm, tight). Further: If God hides His countenance, i.e., is angry and punishes, who can then behold Him, i.e., make Him, the veiled One, visible and claim back the favour withdrawn? The <hi type="italic">Waw</hi> of וּמי, if one marks off the periods of the paratactic expression, is in both cases the <hi type="italic">Waw</hi> of conclusion after hypothetical antecedents, and. <hi type="italic"><reference osisRef="Job.34.29">Job 34:29</reference></hi> refers to Job’s impetuous challenging of God. Thus exalted above human controversy and defiance, God rules both over the mass and over individuals alike. יחד gives intensity of the equality thus correlatively (<hi type="italic">et-et</hi>) expressed (Targ., Syr.); to refer it to אדם as generalizing (lxx, Jer. <hi type="italic">et super omnes homines</hi>), is forbidden by the antithesis of peoples and individuals. To the thought, that God giveth rest (from oppressors) and hides His countenance (from the oppressors and in general those who act wrongly), two co-ordinate negative final clauses are attached: in order that godless men may not rule (ממּלך, as e.g., 2Ki 23:33, <hi type="italic">Keri</hi>), in order that they may no longer be (מ( e = מהיות, under the influence of the notion of putting aside contained in the preceding final clause, therefore like <reference osisRef="Isa.7.8">Isa 7:8</reference> מעם, <reference osisRef="Isa.24.2">Isa 24:2</reference> מעיר, <reference osisRef="Jer.48.2">Jer 48:2</reference> מגוי, and the like) snares of the people, i.e., those whose evil example and bad government become the ruin of the community. <div eID="gen8455" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen8456" type="x-p"/> In <hi type="italic"><reference osisRef="Job.34.31">Job 34:31</reference></hi> the view of those who by some jugglery concerning the laws of the vowel sounds explain האמר as imper. <hi type="italic">Niph</hi>. (= האמר), be it in the sense of להאמר, <hi type="italic">dicendum est</hi> (Rosenm., Schlottm., and others, after Raschi), or even in the unheard-of reflexive signification: express thyself (Stick., Hahn), is to be rejected. The syncopated form of the <hi type="italic">infin</hi>. בּהרג, <reference osisRef="Ezek.26.15">Eze 26:15</reference>, does not serve as a palliation of this adventurous imperative. It is, on the contrary, אמר with ה <hi type="italic">interrog.,</hi> as <reference osisRef="Ezek.28.9">Eze 28:9</reference> האמר, and probably also העמוּר Mic 2:7 (vid., Hitz.). A direct exhortation to Job to penitence would also not be in place here, although what Elihu says is levelled against Job. The כּי is confirmatory. Thus God acts with that class of unscrupulous men who abuse their power for the destruction of their subjects: for he (one of them) says (or: has said, from the standpoint of the execution of punishment) to God, etc. Ew. differently: “for one says thus to God even: I expiate what I do not commit,” by understanding the speech quoted of a defiance which reproachfully demands an explanation. It is, however, manifestly a compendious model confession. And since Elihu with כי establishes the execution of punishment from this, that it never entered the mind of the עדם חנף thus to humble himself before God, so נשׂאתי here cannot signify: I have repented (put up with and had to bear what I have deserved); on the contrary, the confession begins with the avowal: I have exalted myself (נשׂא, <hi type="italic">se efferre,</hi> in Hos 13:1; <reference osisRef="Ps.89.10">Psa 89:10</reference>), which is then followed by the vow: I will not (in the future) do evil (חבל synon. עוה, as <reference osisRef="Neh.1.7">Neh 1:7</reference>, and probably also <hi type="italic">supra</hi>, <reference osisRef="Job.24.9">Job 24:9</reference>), and the entreaty, <reference osisRef="Job.34.32">Job 34:32</reference> : beside that which I behold (elliptical object-clause, Ew. §333, <hi type="italic">b</hi>), i.e., what lies beyond my vision (= נסתּרות or עלמים, <reference osisRef="Ps.19.13">Psa 19:13</reference>; <reference osisRef="Ps.90.8">Psa 90:8</reference>, unacknowledged sins), teach me; and the present vow has reference to acknowledged sins and sins that have still to be acknowledged: if I have done wrong, I will do it no more. Thus speaking - Elihu means - those high ones might have anticipated the punishment of the All-just God, for favour instead of wrath cannot be extorted, it is only reached by the way of lowly penitence.
entries.e798a88c0bc01f181f65c0d9e42ec1b1c984dcda: Job 34:33-37 33  Shall He recompense it as thou wilt? For thou hast found fault, <div eID="gen8456" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen8457" type="x-p"/> So that thou hast to determine, not I, <div eID="gen8457" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen8458" type="x-p"/> And what thou knowest speak out! 34  Men of understanding will say to me, <div eID="gen8458" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen8459" type="x-p"/> And a wise man who listeneth to me: 35  “Job speaketh without knowledge, “And his words are without intelligence.” 36  O would that Job were proved to the extreme <div eID="gen8459" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen8460" type="x-p"/> On account of his answers after the manner of evil men; 37  For he addeth transgression to his sin, <div eID="gen8460" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen8461" type="x-p"/> Among us he clappeth <div eID="gen8461" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen8462" type="x-p"/> And multiplieth his speeches against God. <div eID="gen8462" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen8463" type="x-p"/> The question put to Job, whether then from him or according to his idea (עם in מעמּך as <reference osisRef="Job.23.10">Job 23:10</reference>; <reference osisRef="Job.27.11">Job 27:11</reference>, which see) shall God recompense it (viz., as this “it” is to be understood according to <hi type="italic"><reference osisRef="Job.34.32">Job 34:32</reference></hi>: man’s evil-doing and actions in general), Elihu proves from this, that Job has despised (shown himself discontented with it) the divine mode of recompense, so that therefore (this second כּי signifies also <hi type="italic">nam</hi>, but is, because extending further on account of the first, according to the sense equivalent to <hi type="italic">ita ut</hi>) he has to choose (seek out) another mode of recompense, not Elihu (who is perfectly satisfied with the mode with which history furnishes us); which is then followed by the challenge (דּבּר not <hi type="italic">infin.,</hi> but as <reference osisRef="Job.33.32">Job 33:32</reference>): what (more corresponding to just retribution) thou knowest, speak out then! Elihu on his part knows that he does not stand alone against Job, the censurer of the divine government of the world, but that men of heart (understanding) and (every) wise man who listens to him will coincide with him in the opinion that Job’s talk is devoid of knowledge and intelligence (on the form of writing השׂכּיל as <reference osisRef="Jer.3.15">Jer 3:15</reference>, vid., Ges. §53, rem. 2). <div eID="gen8463" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen8464" type="x-p"/> In <reference osisRef="Job.34.36">Job 34:36</reference> we will for the present leave the meaning of אבי undecided; יבּחן is certainly intended as optative: let Job be tried to the extreme or last, i.e., let his trial by affliction continue until the matter is decided (comp. <reference osisRef="Hab.1.4">Hab 1:4</reference>), on account of the opposition among men of iniquity, i.e., after the manner of such (on this Beth of association comp. בּקּשׁשׁים, <reference osisRef="Job.36.14">Job 36:14</reference>), for to חטּאת, by which the purpose of his affliction is to be cleared up, he adds פּשׁע, viz., the wickedness of blasphemous speeches: among us (therefore without fear) he claps (viz., his hands scornfully together, יספּוק only here thus absolute instead of ישׂפּק כּפּיו fo dae, <reference osisRef="Job.27.23">Job 27:23</reference>, comp. בשׂפק <reference osisRef="Job.36.18">Job 36:18</reference> with ספקו <reference osisRef="Job.20.22">Job 20:22</reference>)<note placement="foot">The mode of writing with ס instead of שׂ is limited in the book of Job, according to the Masora, to <reference osisRef="Job.34.26">Job 34:26</reference>, Job 34:37.</note> and multiplies (ירב, <hi type="italic">fut. apoc. Hiph.</hi> as <reference osisRef="Job.10.17">Job 10:17</reference>, and instead of the full fut., as ישׂר, <reference osisRef="Job.33.27">Job 33:27</reference>) his speeches against God, i.e., exceeds himself in speeches which irreverently dictate to and challenge God. <div eID="gen8464" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen8465" type="x-p"/> But we now ask, what does that אבי, <hi type="italic"><reference osisRef="Job.34.36">Job 34:36</reference></hi>, signify? According to the accentuation with <hi type="italic">Rebia</hi>, it appears to be intended to signify <hi type="italic">pater mi</hi> (Jer.), according to which Saad. (<hi type="italic">jâ rabbı̂</hi>) and Gecat. (<hi type="italic">munchiı̂</hi>, my Creator) translate it. This would be the only passage where an Old Testament saint calls God אבי; elsewhere God is called the Father of Israel, and Israel as a people, or the individual comprehending himself with the nation, calls Him אבינו. Nevertheless this <hi type="italic">pater mi</hi> for Elihu would not be inappropriate, for what the writer of the Epistle to the Hebrews, <reference osisRef="Heb.12.7">Heb 12:7</reference>, says to believers on the ground of <reference osisRef="Prov.3.11">Pro 3:11</reference> : εἰς παιδείαν ὑπομένετε, ye suffer for the purpose of paternal discipline, is Elihu’s fundamental thought; he also calls God in <reference osisRef="Job.32.22">Job 32:22</reference>; <reference osisRef="Job.36.3">Job 36:3</reference>, which a like reference to himself, עשׂני and פעלי - this ejaculatory “my Father!” especially in conjunction with the following wish, remains none the less objectionable, and only in the absence of a more agreeable interpretation should we, with Hirz., decide in its favour. It would be disproportionately repulsive if <reference osisRef="Job.34.36">Job 34:36</reference> still belonged to the assenting language of another, and Elihu represented himself as addressed by אבי (Wolfson, Maur.). Thus, therefore, אבי must be taken somehow or other interjectionally. It is untenable to compare it with אבוי, <reference osisRef="Prov.23.29">Pro 23:29</reference>, for אוי ואבוי (Arab. <hi type="italic">âh wa - âwâh</hi>) is “ah! and alas!” The Aramaic בייא בייא, <hi type="italic">vae vae</hi> (Buxtorf, col. 294), compared by Ges. to בּי, signifies just the same. The Targ. translates צבינא, I wish; after which Kimchi, among moderns, Umbr., Schlottm., Carey, and others derive אבי from אבה, a wish (after the form קצה, הזה), but the participial substantival-form badly suits this signification, which is at once improbable according to the usage of the language so far as we at present know it. This interpretation also does not well suit the בי, which is to be explained at the same time. Ewald, §358, <hi type="italic">a</hi>, regards אבי as the fuller form of בּי, and thinks אבי is dialectic = לבי = לוי = לוּ, but this is an etymological leger-demain. The two Schultens (died 1750 and 1793) were on the right track when they traced back אבי to בוא, but their interpretation: <hi type="italic">rem eo adducam ut</hi> (אבי = אביא, as it is certainly not unfrequently written, e.g., 1Ki 21:29, with the assumption of a root בי cognate with בא), is artificial and without support in the usage of the language and in the syntax. Körber and Simonis opened up the right way, but with inadequate means for following it out, by referring (vid., Ges. <hi type="italic">Thes. s.v.</hi> בּי) to the formula of a wish and of respect, <hi type="italic">bawwâk allah ,</hi> which, however, also is <hi type="italic">bajjâk</hi>. The Kamus interprets <hi type="italic">bajjâk</hi>, though waveringly, by <hi type="italic">bawwâk</hi>, the meaning of which (may he give thee a resting-place) is more transparent. In an annotated Codex of Zamachschari <hi type="italic">hajjâk allah wa - bajjâk</hi> is explained: God preserve thy life and grant thee to come to a place of rest, <hi type="italic">bawwaaka</hi> (therefore Arab. <hi type="italic">bawâ</hi> = <hi type="italic">bawa'a</hi>) <hi type="italic">menzilan</hi>. That אבי (as also בּי) is connected with this <hi type="italic">bajjâk</hi> since the latter is the <hi type="italic">Piel</hi>-form of an old verb <hi type="italic">bajja</hi> (vid., <hi type="italic">supra</hi>, p. 559), which with the forms Arab. <hi type="italic">bâ'a</hi> (whence Arab. <hi type="italic">bı̂‛at</hi>, a sheltering house) and Arab. <hi type="italic">bw'</hi> (<hi type="italic">bwâ</hi>) has one root similar in signification with בוא, the following contributions of Wetzstein will show. <div eID="gen8465" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen8466" type="x-p"/> In elucidation of the present passage he observes: The expressions <hi type="italic">abı̂ tebı̂ , jebı̂ ; nebı̂ , tebû , jebû ,</hi> are so frequent in Damascus, that they very soon struck me, and on my first inquiry I always received the same answer, that they are a mutilation of Arab. <hi type="italic">'bgy , abghi ,</hi> I desire, etc. [<hi type="italic">vid. supra,</hi> p. 580], until one day a fugitive came into the consulate, and with these words, <hi type="italic">abı̂ wâlidêk</hi>, seized me in that part of the body where the Arabs wear the girdle (<hi type="italic">zunnâr</hi>), a symbolic action by which one seeks some one’s protection. Since the word here could not be equivalent to <hi type="italic">abghi</hi> (“I desire” thy parents), I turned to the person best acquainted with the idiom of the country, the scribe <hi type="italic">Abderrahmân</hi> <hi type="italic">el-Mîdâni, </hi>which father had been a wandering minstrel in the camps for twenty years; and he explained to me that <hi type="italic">abghi</hi> only signifies “I desire;” on the contrary, <hi type="italic">abı̂</hi>, “I implore importunately, I pray for God’s sake,” and the latter belongs to a defective verb, Arab. <hi type="italic">bayya</hi>, from which, except the forms mentioned, only the part. <hi type="italic">anâ bâj ,</hi> “I come as a suppliant,” and its plur. <hi type="italic">nahn bâjin ,</hi> is used. The poet <hi type="italic">Musa Rârâ</hi> from <hi type="italic">Krêje</hi> in the south of Hauran, who lived with me six months in Damascus in order to instruct me in the dialect of his district, assured me that among the Beduins also the <hi type="italic">perf</hi>. forms <hi type="italic">bı̂t , bı̂nâ</hi> (I have, we have entreated), and the <hi type="italic">fut</hi>. forms <hi type="italic">tabı̂n</hi> (thou, woman ... ), <hi type="italic">jaben</hi> (they, the women ... ), and <hi type="italic">taben</hi> (ye women ... ), are used. In the year 1858, in the course of a journey in his native country, I came to <hi type="italic">Dîmâs</hi>, whither they had brought two strange Beduins who had been robbed of their horses in that desert (<hi type="italic">Sahra Dîmâs</hi>), and one of them had at the same time received a mortal gunshot-wound. As I can to these men, who were totally forsaken, the wounded man began to express his importunate desire for a surgeon with the words <hi type="italic">jâ shêch nebı̂ ‛arabak</hi>, “Sir, we claim the protection of thy Arabs,” i.e., we adjure thee by thy family. Naturally <hi type="italic">abı̂</hi> occurs most frequently. It generally has its obj. in the <hi type="italic">acc.,</hi> often also with the <hi type="italic">praepos</hi>. Arab. <hi type="italic">‛ly ,</hi> exactly like Arab. <hi type="italic">dchl</hi> (to enter, to flee anywhere and hide), which is its correct synonym and usual substitute in common life. It is often used without an obj., and, indeed, very variously. With women it is chiefly the introduction to a question prompted by curiosity, as: <hi type="italic">abı̂</hi> (ah, tell me), have you really betrothed your daughter? Or the word is accompanied by a gesture by the five fingers of the right hand, with the tips united, being stretched out towards the hasty or impatient listener, as if one wished to show some costly object, when <hi type="italic">abı̂</hi> signifies as much as: I pray thee wait till I have shown thee this precious thing, i.e., allow me to make one more remark to thee in reference to the matter. Moreover, בּי (probably not corrupted from אבי, but a derived <hi type="italic">nomen concretum</hi> in the sense of <hi type="italic">dachı̂ l</hi> or <hi type="italic">mustagı̂r</hi>, one seeking protection, protégé, after the form אי, צי, from בוה = בוא) still exists unaltered in Hauran and in the steppe. The Beduin introduces an important request with the words <hi type="italic">anâ bı̂ ahlak</hi>, I am a protégé of thy family, or <hi type="italic">anâ bı̂ ‛irdak</hi>, I trust to thine honour, etc.; while in Damascus they say, <hi type="italic">anâ dachı̂l ahlak , harı̂mak , aulâdak ,</hi> etc. The Beduin women make use of this <hi type="italic">bı̂</hi> in a weakened signification, in order to beg a piece of soap or sugar, and <hi type="italic">anâ bı̂ lihjetak ,</hi> I pray by thy beard, etc., is often heard. <div eID="gen8466" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen8467" type="x-p"/> If now we combine that אבי of Elihu with <hi type="italic">abghi</hi> (from Arab. <hi type="italic">bgâ</hi>, Hebr. בּעה, Aram. בּעא, <hi type="italic">fut</hi>. יבעי, as בּי with בּעי) or with <hi type="italic">abî</hi> = אבא, from the verb <hi type="italic">bajja</hi> = בוא (בי),<note placement="foot">We cannot in any case, with Wetzst., explain the אבי אבי,   2Ki 2:12; 2Ki 13:14, according to the above, so that the king of Israel adjured the dying prophet by the national army and army of the faithful not to forsake him, as an Arab is now and then adjured in most urgent and straitened circumstances “by the army of Islam;” vid., on the other hand, 2Ki 6:21, comp. <reference osisRef="Job.5.13">Job 5:13</reference>; <reference osisRef="Job.8.9">Job 8:9</reference> (בּנך). Here rather, if an Arabian parallel be needed, the usual death wail, <hi type="italic">bi - abı̂ anta</hi> (thou wast dear as a father to me), e.g., in Kosegarten, <hi type="italic">Chrestom</hi>. p. 140, 3, is to be compared. אבי,   <reference osisRef="1Sam.24.12">1Sa 24:12</reference>, might more readily, with Ew. §101, <hi type="italic">c</hi>, be brought in here and regarded as belonging to the North Palestine peculiarities of the book of Kings; but by a comparison of the passages cited, this is also improbable.</note> it always remains a remarkable instance in favour of the Arabic colouring of the Elihu section similar to the rest of the book, - a colouring, so to speak, dialectically Hauranitish; while, on the other hand, even by this second speech, one cannot avoid the impression of a great distance between it and the rest of the book: the language has a lofty tone, without its special harshness, as there, being the necessary consequence of a carefully concentrated fulness of thought; moreover, here in general the usual regularity of the strophe-lines no longer prevails, and also the usual symmetrical balance of thought in them. <div eID="gen8467" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen8468" type="x-p"/> If we confine our attention to the real substance of the speech, apart from the emotional and rough accessories, Elihu casts back the reproach of injustice which Job has raised, first as being contradictory to the being of God, Job 34:10.; then he seeks to refute it as contradicting God’s government, and this he does (1) apagogically from the unselfish love with which God’s protecting care preserves the breath of every living thing, while He who has created all things might bring back all created things to the former non-existence, <reference osisRef="Job.34.12-Job.15.2">Job 34:12-15; (2</reference>) by induction from the impartial judgment which He exercises over princes and peoples, and from which it is inferred that the Ruler of the world is also all-just, <reference osisRef="Job.34.16">Job 34:16</reference>-20. From this Elihu proves that God can exercise justice, and from that, that He is omniscient, and sees into man’s inmost nature without any judicial investigation, <reference osisRef="Job.34.21-Job.34.28">Job 34:21-28</reference>; inaccessible to human accusation and human defiance, He rules over peoples and individuals, even over kings, and nothing turns His just punishment aside but lowly penitence blended with the prayer for the disclosure of unperceived sin, <reference osisRef="Job.34.29">Job 34:29</reference>-32. For in His retributive rule God does not follow the discontented demands of men arrogant and yet devoid of counsel, Job 34:33. It is worthy of recognition, that Elihu does not here coincide with what has been already said (especially <reference osisRef="Job.12.15">Job 12:15</reference>), without applying it to another purpose; and that his theodicy differs essentially from that proclaimed by the friends. It is not derived from mere appearance, but lays hold of the very principles. It does not attempt the explanation of the many apparent contradictions to retributive justice which outward events manifest, as agreeing with it; it does not solve the question by mere empiricism, but from the idea of the Godhead and its relation to the world, and by such inner necessity guarantees to the mysteries still remaining to human shortsightedness, their future solution.  <chapter eID="Job.34"/> <div eID="gen8468" type="x-p"/>

                  <ns0:p n="1">1. FUrthermore, Elihu answered, and said,</ns0:p>
                  <ns0:p n="2">2. Hear my words, O ye wise men <ns0:note n="a" place="bottom">Who are here present: do you judge of the truth and reason of what I have said, and am further to say: for I am willing to submit all to the judgment of the truly wise.</ns0:note>, and give ear unto me, ye that have knowledge.</ns0:p>
                  <ns0:p n="3">3. <ns0:note n="*" place="margin">Chap. 6. 30. & 12. 11.</ns0:note> For the ear trieth words <ns0:note n="b" place="bottom">
                        <ns0:hi>i. e.</ns0:hi> Man's mind judgeth of things spoken and heard. <ns0:hi>The ear,</ns0:hi> the sense of Discipline is put for the mind to which things are con<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />veyed by it. See the note on <ns0:hi>Iob</ns0:hi> 12. 11.</ns0:note>, as the <ns0:note n="†" place="margin">
                        <ns0:hi>Heb.</ns0:hi> palate.</ns0:note> mouth tasteth meat.</ns0:p>
                  <ns0:p n="4">4. Let us choose to us judgment <ns0:note n="c" place="bottom">
                        <ns0:hi>i. e.</ns0:hi> Justice and Equity, <ns0:hi>judgment</ns0:hi> being oft synecdochically used for just judgment, as <ns0:hi>Iob</ns0:hi> 8. 3. & 19 7. & 32. 9. <ns0:hi>Psal.</ns0:hi> 37. 28. Let us not contend for victory, but only for Truth and Justice. This shall be my only care and business. Let us lay aside all pre<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />judices and animosities, which I perceive have had too great an in<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />fluence upon thee and thy friends, and impartially consider the naked truth and right of the cause.</ns0:note>: let us know <ns0:note n="d" place="bottom">
                        <ns0:hi>i. e.</ns0:hi> Let us discover or make it known one to another.</ns0:note> among our selves what <ns0:hi>is</ns0:hi> good <ns0:note n="e" place="bottom">Who hath the best cause.</ns0:note>:</ns0:p>
                  <ns0:p n="5">5. For Job hath said, <ns0:note n="*" place="margin">Chap. <ns0:gap reason="illegible" resp="#APEX" extent="1 word">
                           <ns0:desc>〈◊〉</ns0:desc>
                        </ns0:gap>
                     </ns0:note> I am righteous <ns0:note n="f" place="bottom">Either 1. I am perfectly righteous. But this <ns0:hi>Iob</ns0:hi> did not say, but the contrary, <ns0:hi>Iob</ns0:hi> 9. 2, 3. & 14. 4. Or 2. I am a sincere Per<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />son, no Hypocrite, as my Friends make me. But this <ns0:hi>Elibu</ns0:hi> doth not deny. or 3. I am so far righteous, and have been so holy and blameless in my life, that I have not deserved, not had any reason to expect such hard usage from God. And this <ns0:hi>Iob</ns0:hi> had oft inti<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />mated, and <ns0:hi>Elihu</ns0:hi> doth justly blame him for it, that he blazoned his own righteousness with tacit reflections upon God for dealing so severely with him.</ns0:note>: and my God hath taken away my judgment <ns0:note n="g" place="bottom">For so <ns0:hi>Iob</ns0:hi> had said, Ch. 27. 2. <ns0:hi>i. e.</ns0:hi> He denies me that which is but just and equal, to give me a fair hear<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />ing, to suffer me to plead my Cause with or before him, to shew me the reasons of his contending with me, and what sins besides com<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />mon infirmities, I have been guilty of whereby I have deserved such extraordinary judgments. Which <ns0:hi>Elihu</ns0:hi> justly taxeth him with as a very irreverent and presumptuous expression.</ns0:note>.</ns0:p>
